title: Agilent 1260 Infinity Binary LC System User Guide
locator: Chapter 1, System Components. Chapter 5, Preparing the System (p. 83), Data Acquisition (p. 88) and Data Analysis (p. 96).
summary: Agilent identifies the G1312B binary pump and G4212B diode array detector in its system description. The quick start explains how to prepare the system, acquire chromatograms and analyze the recorded peaks.
scope: Covers the original 1260 Infinity Binary LC configuration. Sample preparation, detector wavelength, column choice and calibration depend on the assay.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to Agilent's copyrighted system guide.

title: Determination of Caffeine in Coffee Products According to DIN 20481
locator: Page 2, Equipment and HPLC method. Figure 1, calibrations. Table 1, precision. Figures 4–5, instant coffee samples.
summary: Agilent measured caffeine in regular and decaffeinated instant coffee using a 1260 Infinity with a binary pump and diode array detection at 272 nm. The peak-area calibrations covered 1.25–20 mg/L for regular coffee extracts and 0.125–4 mg/L for decaffeinated extracts.
scope: This application uses an isocratic C18 separation. Figures 4 and 5 distinguish concentration in the extract (mg/L) from content in the original granules (mg/g). The equipment list identifies the original 1260 Infinity as the system used for the measurements.
rights: Original catalog summary with a link to Agilent's application note.

title: Determination of caffeine content in coffee drinks prepared in some coffee shops in the local market in Jeddah City, Saudi Arabia
locator: Section 2, instrumentation and standards. Table 1, calibration statistics. Tables 2–3, coffee results.
summary: Al-Baqami and colleagues compared coffees using a Shimadzu UFLC system with an LC-20AD pump and a C18 column. A caffeine standard series from 5 to 45 µg/mL gave a peak-area calibration with R² of 0.9996. They reported a quantification limit of 3.619 µg/mL.
scope: Independent calibration evidence for the reported Shimadzu configuration. Its sensitivity applies to that detector, column and method. Table 2 compares the sampled drinks using the authors' preparation and dilution.
rights: Original summary of Al-Baqami et al. The authors publish the article under CC BY 4.0.

title: Determination of the caffeine contents of various food items within the Austrian market and validation of a caffeine assessment tool (CAT)
publisher: Food Additives & Contaminants: Part A, Taylor & Francis
locator: Authors' abstract, analytical method and beverage results, journal pages 1849–1860.
summary: Rudolph, Färbinger and König analyzed 124 foods and drinks by reversed-phase HPLC with UV detection after solid-phase extraction. The sampled energy drinks contained 266–340 mg/L caffeine. Tea and iced tea covered 13–183 mg/L.
scope: These concentrations describe a market survey. They can help put a beverage measurement in context. The extract cleanup and product matrix matter when considering transfer to a local assay.
rights: Original catalog summary based on the authors' abstract in the University of Vienna repository.

title: Determination of Seven Artificial Sweeteners in Diet Food Preparations by Reverse-Phase Liquid Chromatography with Absorbance Detection
publisher: Journal of the Association of Official Analytical Chemists
locator: Authors' abstract, matrix preparation and detector selection, journal pages 934–937.
summary: This published C18 gradient method covers seven sweeteners in diet drinks and food preparations. Liquid samples were diluted and filtered. Several sweeteners were measured by UV at 200 or 210 nm, while cyclamate required an additional post-column extraction.
scope: The measured compounds and the sample matrix determine the preparation and detector needed. The authors reported no interference from the caffeine, benzoic acid and sorbic acid tested, and could not detect stevioside or talin.
rights: Original catalog summary based on the authors' abstract hosted by the journal.
